title: The Shield
summary: Put a 220 Ohm resistor in front of the LED so it glows instead of dying. One part, one calculation, and the LED lives forever.

briefing.text: Same circuit as last time, but this run the LED survives. All it needs is one resistor standing between it and the 5 V rail.
A resistor in series sets the current for the whole loop. Pick 220 Ohm and you get a bright, safe 14 mA.

learn.title: Sizing the current-limiting resistor
learn.body:
The LED drops a fixed forward voltage Vf. Everything left over lands on the resistor, and the resistor decides the current:

    I = (Vsrc - Vf) / (R + Rpin + rOn)

Rearranged to pick a resistor for a target current:

    R = (Vsrc - Vf) / I

For a red LED on 5 V at a comfortable 20 mA:

    R = (5 V - 1.8 V) / 0.020 A = 160 Ohm

There is no 160 Ohm in the drawer, so go up to the next standard value: 220 Ohm. Going up is always safe — a bigger resistor means less current and a slightly dimmer, longer-lived LED. Measured here: about 13.9 mA, roughly 83 % brightness.

objectives.text: Keep 5 V on the red rail and GND on the blue rail

hints.tier1: The power jumpers from the last level still do their job — leave them where they are.

tier2.text: 5V to the red rail, GND to the blue rail.

objectives.text: Put a 220 Ohm resistor between the 5 V rail and the LED anode

hints.tier1: In series means the current has no choice but to go through both parts. The resistor must sit in the wire, not beside it.

tier2.text: One end of the resistor on the rail side, the other end in the same row as the LED anode.

objectives.text: Return the LED cathode to ground

hints.tier1: Current only flows in a complete loop. The short leg of the LED needs a way back to GND.

tier2.text: Jumper the cathode's row to the blue rail.

objectives.text: Run it: the LED glows brightly and nothing is damaged

hints.tier1: If the LED is dark, check its direction — the anode must face the positive side. If it blew, press Reset sim after adding the resistor.

tier2.text: 220 Ohm from 5 V gives about 13.9 mA, which is a safe, bright glow.

starCriteria.threeText: Do it with exactly two parts: one resistor and one LED

successText: Steady, bright, and cool to the touch. About 13.9 mA of the 20 mA the LED can take — that resistor will keep it alive for twenty years.
chipOnSmoke: Still smoking? The current is finding a way around the resistor. Make sure the resistor is in the path, not bridging the same row as the LED anode.
